q: Several capacitors can be connected together to be used in a variety of applications.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. Several capacitors can be connected together to be used in a variety of applications.

q: There are three types of capacitor combinations namely; parallel, series, and diagonal.
e: False. The right claim is this: There are two types of combination namely; parallel and series. In series, the same current runs through each part and the voltages add. The printed line wrongly says there are three types of capacitor combinations namely; parallel, series, and diagonal.

q: In capacitors connected in parallel, the plates connected together at one point have positive charges and at the other point have negative charges.
e: True. In parallel, the same voltage sits across each branch and the currents add. Point have positive charges and at the other point have negative charges.

q: In a parallel combination, all the capacitors have different potential differences.
e: False. The right claim is this: In a series combination, the capacitors have different potential differences. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. The printed line wrongly says in a parallel combination, all the capacitors have different potential differences.

q: In a parallel combination, all the capacitors carry the same amount of charge.
e: False. The right claim is this: In a parallel combination, all the capacitors have the same potential difference. Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. The printed line wrongly says in a parallel combination, all the capacitors carry the same amount of charge.

q: If the potential difference of each capacitor in parallel is V, the charge on a capacitor is $Q = \frac{V}{C}$.
e: False. The right claim is this: If the potential difference of the capacitor is 1 V when it is given a charge 1 C, its capacitance is 1 F. Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. The printed line wrongly says if the potential difference of each capacitor in parallel is V, the charge on a capacitor is Q = (V)/(C).

q: The total charge Q on capacitors in parallel is the sum of the individual charges: $Q = Q_1 + Q_2 + Q_3$.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. The relation in this line is Q = Q1 + Q2 + Q3.

q: We can replace capacitors in parallel with a single equivalent capacitor provided it has the same total charge Q when the same potential difference V is applied.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. Same total charge Q when the same potential difference V is applied.

q: The equivalent capacitance of capacitors connected in parallel is the product of the individual capacitances.
e: False. The right claim is this: The equivalent capacitance of capacitors connected in parallel is the sum of the individual capacitances. Parallel capacitors share voltage, charges add, and equivalent C is the sum. The printed line wrongly says the equivalent capacitance of capacitors connected in parallel is the product of the individual capacitances.

q: For n capacitors in parallel, the equivalent capacitance is $C = C_1 + C_2 + C_3 + ... + C_n$.
e: True. Parallel capacitors share voltage, charges add, and equivalent C is the sum. The relation in this line is C = C1 + C2 + C3 +.

q: The equivalent capacitance C of the parallel combination of n identical capacitors, each of capacitance C, is $C = \frac{C}{n}$.
e: False. The right claim is this: The equivalent capacitance C of the parallel combination of n identical capacitors, each of capacitance C1, is C = n C1. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. The printed line wrongly says the equivalent capacitance C of the parallel combination of n identical capacitors, each of capacitance C, is C = (C)/(n).

q: In capacitors connected in series, the negatively charged plate of one capacitor is connected to the positively charged plate of the other.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. One capacitor is connected to the positively charged plate of the other.

q: Since the capacitors are connected in series, each capacitor has a different charge.
e: False. The right claim is this: Since the capacitors are connected in series each capacitor has the same charge. In series, the same current runs through each part and the voltages add. The printed line wrongly says since the capacitors are connected in series, each capacitor has a different charge.

q: In a series combination, the capacitors have different potential differences.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. In a series combination, the capacitors have different potential differences.

q: The total potential difference V of a series capacitor combination is the sum of the individual potential differences: $V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$.
e: True. Series capacitors share charge, voltages add, and equivalent C is smaller than the smallest. The relation in this line is V = V1 + V2 + V3.

q: For capacitors in series, the potential difference across an individual capacitor is $V = QC$.
e: False. The right claim is this: The total potential difference V of a series capacitor combination is the reciprocal of individual potential differences. Series capacitors share charge, voltages add, and equivalent C is smaller than the smallest. The printed line wrongly says for capacitors in series, the potential difference across an individual capacitor is V = QC.

q: The charge of the equivalent capacitor in series is Q when the total potential difference V is applied.
e: True. In series, the same current runs through each part and the voltages add. In series is Q when the total potential difference V is applied.

q: When capacitors are connected in series, the reciprocal of the equivalent capacitance is the sum of the reciprocals of their individual capacitances.
e: True. Series capacitors share charge, voltages add, and equivalent C is smaller than the smallest. Equivalent capacitance is the sum of the reciprocals of their individual capacitances.

q: The formula for equivalent capacitance of n capacitors in series is $C = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + ... + \frac{1}{C_n}$.
e: False. The right claim is this: For n capacitors in parallel, the equivalent capacitance is C = C1 + C2 + C3 + . + Cn. In parallel, the same voltage sits across each branch and the currents add.

q: The equivalent capacitance $C_s$ of the series combination of n identical capacitors, each of capacitance C, is $C_s = \frac{C}{n}$.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. The relation in this line is Cs = (C)/(n).

q: In a series connection of capacitors, the total equivalent capacitance is always greater than the largest individual capacitance.
e: False. The right claim is this: In a parallel connection of capacitors, the total equivalent capacitance is always greater than the largest individual capacitance. In parallel, the same voltage sits across each branch and the currents add. The printed line wrongly says in a series connection of capacitors, the total equivalent capacitance is always greater than the largest individual capacitance.

q: In a parallel connection of capacitors, the total equivalent capacitance is always greater than the largest individual capacitance.
e: True. In parallel, the same voltage sits across each branch and the currents add. The total equivalent capacitance is always greater than the largest individual capacitance.

q: If two capacitors are connected in series, the magnitude of charge on the combination is received equally by the individual capacitors.
e: True. In series, the same current runs through each part and the voltages add. Of charge on the combination is received equally by the individual capacitors.

q: In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across each capacitor depends on its capacitance.
e: False. The right claim is this: If the potential difference of the capacitor is 1 V when it is given a charge 1 C, its capacitance is 1 F. One farad is one coulomb per volt, so practical capacitors are µF, nF or pF. The printed line wrongly says in a parallel circuit, the potential difference across each capacitor depends on its capacitance.

q: The equivalent capacitance is defined as the capacitance of a single capacitor that can replace the combination without changing the total charge and potential difference.
e: True. Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. Can replace the combination without changing the total charge and potential difference.
